chunks.text: Mangifera indica, the common mango, is a large evergreen tree that originated in the region covering present-day northeastern India, Myanmar and Bangladesh, and has since become one of the world's most widely grown tropical fruit trees. Mature trees reach 30-40 m with a crown radius of 10-15 m and a taproot that can run 6 m deep in good soil; some specimens are still fruiting after roughly 300 years. New leaves emerge orange-pink, turn glossy red and then settle into dark green, while the small, five-petalled, mildly fragrant flowers are borne in large terminal panicles. Fruit size and colour vary enormously by cultivar, from about 140 g to 2 kg, and over 500 named cultivars exist, including 'Alphonso' (prized in India as the 'king of mangoes') and 'Tommy Atkins', the workhorse of the global export trade developed in Florida in 1940. India alone accounts for roughly 43% of world production of mangoes, mangosteens and guavas (2023 figures). Culturally, the mango is India's national fruit and Bangladesh's national tree: Emperor Ashoka ordered mango groves planted along roads, Mughal emperor Akbar reputedly planted a 100,000-tree orchard near Darbhanga, and mango leaves are still used in Hindu festival decorations such as Vasant Panchami and Ganesh Chaturthi. The paisley motif found across South Asian textiles is named after the shape of an unripe mango.

chunks.source: Purdue University Center for New Crops & Plant Products — Morton, J., 'Fruits of Warm Climates' (Mango)
chunks.text: Julia Morton's classic horticultural monograph describes the mango as a long-lived tree, 10-30 m tall, whose peach-like but markedly more fibrous flesh surrounds a single large flattened stone; some trees are reported to still bear fruit at roughly 300 years of age. The species is native to southern Asia, particularly eastern India, Myanmar and the Andaman Islands, where it has been cultivated since antiquity. Its global spread is credited to several waves of human movement: Buddhist monks are thought to have carried it to Malaya and eastern Asia, Persian traders to East Africa, and Portuguese traders onward to West Africa and Brazil, from where it reached the West Indies, Mexico, Florida, Hawaii, Australia and South Africa. Florida breeding programmes produced commercial cultivars such as 'Haden', 'Tommy Atkins', 'Keitt' and 'Kent'. Beyond fresh eating, ripe pulp is made into jam, nectar and canned slices, while unripe green fruit goes into chutneys, pickles and relishes; in times of scarcity in India the seed kernel has been roasted, boiled and ground into flour once its tannins are removed. Traditional medicine has used the dried, tannin-rich flowers as an astringent for diarrhoea and dysentery and the bark against rheumatism, and the sap and unripe skin are documented skin irritants, so the text recommends separate knives for peeling and slicing.
